title: When the Glasshouse Burns
premise: Jonah Blackwood has spent eleven years writing postcards to the glasshouse conservatory where her family once lived — an address that burned the night her father's business empire collapsed and her brother disappeared. When the estate is scheduled for auction, Jonah returns as a stranger to bid on a house that no longer legally belongs to anyone she trusts. Sifting through scorched ledgers, a neighbor's testimony, and her own unreliable memories, she discovers the fire was no accident: her brother set it to expose their father's fraud, and paid for it with his freedom and name. In the end, Jonah withdraws from the auction, publishes the letters publicly, and reclaims her own name — choosing memory over property, truth over inheritance.
about_author: Elodie Brightwater is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the papers of defunct estates before turning to fiction. She writes about houses, inheritance, and the people history forgets to bill.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. We meet her in a rented flat, writing weekly postcards to a burned address, working a job she describes like a lodger describing someone else's kitchen. A solicitor's letter arrives: Hollis Glasshouse goes to auction in six weeks. Beat: numb routine cracked open by obligation.

chapters.title: The Tenant of Herself
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She resists returning, drafting excuses, but her postcards begin coming back marked 'addressee unknown' for the first time. Her landlady, Mrs. Okonkwo, gently notes that Jonah never unpacks. Beat: the cost of living unrooted becomes visible.

chapters.title: Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She requests the auction catalogue and finds her childhood home itemized — the glasshouse listed as 'ruin, no reserve.' A photograph shows graffiti on its wall: a word only her brother Theo used. Beat: grief sharpened into purpose; she decides to go back.

chapters.title: Return by Bus
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The journey north through changing landscape mirrors her shifting resolve. She arrives at dusk and sees the glasshouse skeleton against the sky, half-collapsed but unmistakable. Beat: awe and dread braided together; the past made physical again.

chapters.title: The Town That Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, with overheard voices at the village pub. Locals remember the Blackwood fire as scandal and spectacle; versions contradict each other. An old man, Ambrose Pell, watches her too closely. Beat: alienation — she is a stranger in her own history.

chapters.title: Room Nine, The Bell Inn
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She checks into the inn under her mother's maiden name, then lies awake listening to the house settle. Flashback fragments surface: Theo teaching her to name moths in the glasshouse. Beat: tenderness undercut by guilt she can't yet name.

chapters.title: What the Fire Left Standing
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She walks the grounds at dawn, cataloguing what survived: the potting shed, a child's boot print fossilized in concrete, the iron ribs of the glasshouse. She finds a rusted strongbox buried beneath the cold frame. Beat: discovery; the past begins answering back.

chapters.title: Ambrose Pell Knows Things
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Jonah and Ambrose. He was the family's gardener and saw more than he ever said. He recognizes her instantly but says nothing, instead warning her off 'digging.' Beat: wary alliance forming; first hint the fire had witnesses.

chapters.title: The Strongbox
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Inside the box: Theo's notebook, a bank draft made out to a stranger, and a photograph of her father shaking hands with a man she doesn't recognize. The notebook's last entry is dated the night of the fire. Beat: vertigo — the official story starts crumbling.

chapters.title: Father, Ledgered
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV with extended flashback. Reconstructing her father Edmund's rise through Theo's notes: shell companies, falsified provenance for the glasshouse collection itself. She realizes the auction may be selling stolen goods. Beat: disillusionment; power revealed as performance and theft.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She tracks the stranger's identity to Victor Sale, now a respected auctioneer — running this very sale. Confronting him briefly at a preview viewing, she reads his fear beneath his charm. Beat: rising tension; the antagonist enters the frame.

chapters.title: Theo Was Here
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Following clues in the notebook, she finds messages Theo left in the glasshouse mortar and under floorboards — a trail meant for her. His voice returns fully in flashback: funny, furious, certain. Beat: love and heartbreak; the brother restored to her.

chapters.title: What Theo Did
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, pivotal flashback chapter. The full night of the fire: Theo set it deliberately to destroy evidence of Edmund's fraud before investigators could be bought off — and to force their father's hand. Edmund let Theo take the blame. Beat: devastating clarity; the wound finally located.

chapters.title: Where Theo Is Now
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The trail ends at a care facility two counties away: Theo, after prison and a breakdown, lives quietly under a changed name, tending plants. She watches him through a window and cannot make herself knock. Beat: hope colliding with cowardice; the emotional low point before the climb.

chapters.title: Victor Sale Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Victor and Jonah. Victor offers her a settlement to walk away — enough money to vanish comfortably — revealing he knows exactly who she is. His charm curdles into threat. Beat: temptation and menace; the stakes become personal and immediate.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Telephone Call
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A call home: her flat is being sold out from under her; even her exile is unstable. Stripped of retreat, she rereads her years of unsent-feeling postcards and understands they were never letters to a place but to Theo. Beat: resolve crystallizes; she chooses to fight.

chapters.title: The Provenance Papers
chapters.summary: Jonah and Ambrose POV. With Ambrose's testimony and Theo's notebook, she reconstructs proof that the glasshouse collection was fraudulently acquired — making the auction legally and morally poisoned. They copy documents, hide originals. Beat: quiet triumph; the powerless arming themselves with paper.

chapters.title: Night Before the Sale
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Victor's men search her room; the hidden originals survive because Ambrose moved them. Jonah spends the night in the glasshouse ruin among the iron ribs, speaking aloud to Theo for the first time in eleven years. Beat: stillness before storm; grief transmuted into courage.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Multi-POV climax. Jonah stands to bid, then instead reads Theo's final letter aloud to the room, presenting the provenance evidence. Bidders recoil; Victor unravels publicly; the sale collapses amid shouting. Beat: catharsis — truth spoken in the one room built on its suppression.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Falling Glass
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Investigations open; Edmund, ill and diminished, receives her visit and neither apologizes nor denies — she leaves without the absolution she expected. Victor is arrested. Beat: justice without sweetness; the limits of vindication.

chapters.title: The Knock
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She returns to the care facility and knocks. Theo opens the door; recognition is slow, then total. They sit among his plants while she tells him everything, and he tells her what prison took and what survived. Beat: reunion earned, imperfect, real.

chapters.title: Owner of Nothing, Keeper of All
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, coda. The glasshouse is designated a memorial garden rather than sold; Jonah and Theo plant the first bed together. She writes one final postcard — addressed to herself, at her own new address — and finally unpacks. Beat: resolution; identity reclaimed, memory given roots instead of ruins.
